source_text: Ac per hoc eo revolutus es, ut Manichaeum, quem professione contempseras, argumentatione reparares. Nam dicendo: Si mala esset, salvanda non esset speciem pugnandi indueras; subdendo autem: sed si nihil in ea mali esset, salvanda non esset [n250] , ipsi te fideliter militare docuisti. Cum ergo apparuerit hoc tua quod Manichaei sententia contineri, id est malam esse hominum naturam, cui ille et tu pariter inesse malum dicitis, tuque pronuntiaveris malam naturam non esse salvandam, absolutissime confectus est fidem vestram iunctis omnino turmis tam naturam impugnare quam gratiam.
pass_a_gloss: And through this you have been rolled back, that by argumentation you would repair the Manichaean whom you had despised by profession. For by saying: If it were evil, it would not be to be saved, you had put on the appearance of fighting; but by subjecting: but if nothing of evil were in it, it would not be to be saved, you have taught yourself to militate for him faithfully. When therefore it has appeared that this of yours is contained which the sentence of the Manichaean, that is that the nature of humans is evil, to which he and you equally say evil is in, and you have pronounced an evil nature is not to be saved, it has been most absolutely accomplished that your faith with troops altogether joined attacks as much nature as grace.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: Consequently you have come back to restoring by argument the Manichaean whom you despised in your profession. Saying, ‘If it were evil, it ought not to be saved,’ you assumed the appearance of fighting him. Adding, ‘But if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36), you showed that you serve him faithfully. It has therefore become clear that your pronouncement contains the same as Mani’s: human nature is evil, since both you and he say evil exists within it. And you have declared that an evil nature ought not to be saved. It has thus been established completely that your faith, with its forces wholly united to his, attacks both nature and grace.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
